title: The Incense Road: Ancient Trade Across Arabia
summary: How camel caravans carried precious frankincense and myrrh north across Arabia along the Incense Road, how towns such as Hegra grew rich from the trade, and why the route later declined.
poll: Camels were the most important part of the Incense Road.

versions.title: The Incense Road
versions.text:
Long ago, camels went through Arabia. They took a sweet thing to sell. It was frankincense.

It comes from a small tree. It grows in the south. Men cut the bark. Sap drips out. It dries in hard drops. Burn it. It makes a sweet smoke. Myrrh is a sap, too.

Lands like Egypt and Rome wanted it. It made things smell good. They paid a lot for it. It was valuable.

So men took it north to trade. Their path was a trade route. We call it the Incense Road.

Camels did the hard work. A camel can hold a big load. It can go for days with no drink. Men and camels went in a group. It was a caravan. The trip took weeks. It was hard. It was hot.

They stopped at an oasis. It is a spot with water. Towns grew at the stops. The towns got rich. Hegra was one. It is in Saudi Arabia. Its folk cut big tombs in rock.

Then ships took the goods. They went by sea. Few camels used the road.

Now we can go to Hegra. We can see the old tombs.

versions.title: The Incense Road
versions.text:
Over two thousand years ago, long lines of camels walked across the deserts of Arabia. They carried a sweet-smelling treasure called frankincense.

Frankincense is a resin. A resin is a sticky sap. This one comes from a small, tough tree. The tree grows in southern Arabia and parts of Africa. Workers cut the bark, and the milky resin oozes out. It hardens into drops. When burned, they give off a sweet smoke. Myrrh is another sweet resin.

People in faraway lands such as Egypt and Rome wanted these resins for perfume and medicine. They paid a lot for them, so the resins were very valuable.

So merchants carried the resins north along a trade route. It was more than 2,000 kilometers long. It ran up the western side of Arabia to ports on the Mediterranean Sea. Today we call it the Incense Road.

Camels made the journey possible. A camel can carry a heavy load and walk for days without water. Merchants and their camels traveled together in a caravan. The trip took many weeks.

Along the way, each caravan stopped at an oasis for water and rest. Towns such as Najran and Dedan grew at these stops. They grew rich by charging a toll. A toll is a fee that traders paid to pass through. A people called the Nabataeans controlled the northern part of the route. They built the city of Hegra, in what is now Saudi Arabia, and carved huge tombs into its rock.

Later, sailors learned to use seasonal winds to cross the sea. Ships could carry goods for less money. So the land route began to decline.

Today, Hegra is a World Heritage Site, and visitors come to see its tombs.

versions.title: The Incense Road: Ancient Trade Across Arabia
versions.text:
More than two thousand years ago, long lines of camels plodded steadily across the deserts of Arabia, transporting an aromatic treasure called frankincense.

Frankincense is a resin, a sticky sap produced by a small, hardy tree that grows in southern Arabia and parts of northeastern Africa. Workers cut the bark, and the milky resin gradually oozes out. It hardens into drops that release a fragrant smoke when burned. Myrrh is another precious aromatic resin harvested in the same region.

People in distant lands such as Egypt and Rome wanted these resins for perfume and medicine. Because buyers paid such high prices, the resins became extremely valuable.

To satisfy this demand, merchants transported the resins north along a trade route more than 2,000 kilometers long. In reality, it was a network of connected paths that stretched up the western side of the Arabian Peninsula to ports on the Mediterranean Sea, and today it is known as the Incense Road.

Camels, which people in Arabia had domesticated roughly three thousand years ago, made the exhausting journey possible, since a camel can carry a heavy load and travel for days without water. Merchants and their animals journeyed together in a caravan, and the expedition lasted many weeks.

Along the way, each caravan paused at an oasis for water and rest. Settlements such as Najran and Dedan developed at these stops. They became prosperous by charging a toll, a fee that traders paid in exchange for safe passage. A people called the Nabataeans controlled the northern section of the route. Besides their capital, Petra, in present-day Jordan, they constructed the city of Hegra, in what is now Saudi Arabia, carving enormous tombs into its rocky cliffs.

Eventually, sailors learned to use the monsoon, a seasonal wind that changes direction during the year, to cross the sea. Because ships could carry goods more cheaply, the land route began to decline.

In 2008, Hegra became Saudi Arabia's first World Heritage Site, a place recognized as part of humanity's shared heritage, and visitors now travel there to admire its magnificent tombs.

versions.title: The Incense Road: Ancient Trade Across Arabia
versions.text:
More than two thousand years ago, seemingly endless lines of camels plodded steadily across the scorching deserts of Arabia, transporting an aromatic treasure called frankincense that was coveted throughout the ancient world.

Frankincense is a resin, a sticky sap produced by a small, hardy tree that grows in southern Arabia and parts of northeastern Africa. Harvesters deliberately cut the bark, and the milky resin gradually oozes out, solidifying into translucent drops that release a fragrant smoke when burned. Myrrh is another precious aromatic resin harvested in the same region.

Distant civilizations such as Egypt and Rome desired these resins for perfume, cosmetics, and medicine, and because buyers paid such extraordinary prices, the resins became exceptionally valuable.

To satisfy this demand, merchants transported the resins north along a trade route more than 2,000 kilometers long. In reality, it was a network of connected paths that stretched up the western side of the Arabian Peninsula to ports on the Mediterranean Sea, and today it is known as the Incense Road.

Camels, which people in Arabia had domesticated roughly three thousand years ago, made the exhausting journey possible, since a camel can carry a heavy load and travel for days without water. Merchants and their animals journeyed together in a caravan, and the expedition lasted many weeks.

Along the way, each caravan paused at an oasis for water and rest. Settlements such as Najran and Dedan, near present-day AlUla, developed at these stops and became prosperous by charging a toll, a fee that traders paid in exchange for water, protection, and safe passage. A people called the Nabataeans controlled the northern section of the route. Besides their capital, Petra, in present-day Jordan, they constructed the city of Hegra, in what is now Saudi Arabia, carving enormous tombs into its rocky cliffs.

Eventually, sailors learned to use the monsoon, a seasonal wind that changes direction during the year, to cross the sea, and because ships could transport goods more economically, the land route began to decline.

In 2008, Hegra became Saudi Arabia's first World Heritage Site, a place recognized as part of humanity's shared heritage, and visitors now travel there to admire its magnificent tombs.

versions.title: The Incense Road: Ancient Trade Across Arabia
versions.text:
More than two thousand years ago, seemingly endless lines of camels plodded steadily across the scorching deserts of Arabia, transporting an aromatic treasure called frankincense that was coveted throughout the ancient world.

Frankincense is a resin, a sticky substance produced by a small, remarkably hardy tree that flourishes in the arid landscapes of southern Arabia and parts of northeastern Africa. Harvesters deliberately cut the bark, and the milky resin gradually oozes out, solidifying into translucent drops that release a fragrant smoke when burned. Myrrh is another precious aromatic resin harvested in the same region.

Distant civilizations such as Egypt and Rome desired these resins for perfume, cosmetics, and medicine, and because buyers paid such extraordinary prices, the resins became exceptionally valuable.

To satisfy this demand, merchants transported the resins north along a trade route more than 2,000 kilometers long. In reality, it was an intricate network of interconnected paths that stretched up the western side of the Arabian Peninsula to ports on the Mediterranean Sea, and today it is known as the Incense Road.

Camels, which inhabitants of Arabia had domesticated approximately three thousand years ago, made the exhausting journey possible, because a camel can carry a considerable load and travel for days without water. Merchants and their animals journeyed together in a caravan, and the expedition lasted many weeks.

Along the way, each caravan paused at an oasis for water and rest, and settlements such as Najran and Dedan, near present-day AlUla, developed at these stops and became prosperous by charging a toll, a fee that traders paid in exchange for water, protection, and safe passage. A people called the Nabataeans controlled the northern section of the route. Besides their capital, Petra, in present-day Jordan, they constructed the city of Hegra, in what is now Saudi Arabia, carving enormous tombs into its rocky cliffs. Renowned for their ingenious water-management techniques, including underground cisterns that preserved precious rainfall, the Nabataeans accumulated considerable wealth from the commerce traversing their territory.

Eventually, sailors learned to exploit the monsoon, a seasonal wind that reverses direction during the year, to navigate across the sea, and because vessels could transport merchandise more economically, the overland route began to decline gradually.

In 2008, Hegra became Saudi Arabia's first World Heritage Site, a place recognized as part of humanity's shared heritage, and visitors now travel there to admire its magnificent tombs.

HIGH.prompt: Some historians say the Incense Road shaped the history of Arabia. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that the Incense Road shaped the history of Arabia, because it built a lasting network of towns and cities across the region. Merchants carried aromatic resins like frankincense and myrrh along the route, and the tolls they paid let towns such as Najran, Dedan, and Hegra grow wealthy and powerful. The Nabataeans used that wealth to carve the extraordinary tombs of Hegra, a site now honored as a World Heritage location, which shows that the road's influence turned into a heritage still visible today. Even after the monsoon winds let sailors move goods by sea instead, the cities and monuments the road created prove how deeply it shaped Arabia's history.
